messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 24
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Financial Analyst
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath, Avoid Open Spaces: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Hopelessness: I have no future, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mateo Alvarez was 24 when he left the Army and returned to a junior financial analyst job in a glass office tower downtown, but he spoke about the deployment as if the most important part of him had been left there. In session he described one firefight in particular, during a patrol that moved through a wide, exposed stretch of road between damaged buildings. He remembered the brightness first, the flat openness, how visible they all were, and then the crack of gunfire and the chaos that followed. A man from his unit was hit. Mateo could recall certain moments with painful precision—the color of the dust on his friend’s uniform, the sound of someone shouting for cover, the feeling of his own hands moving too fast—yet the sequence would not hold together for him. He would start telling it and then get lost, unsure what came before what, with sharp fragments breaking in out of nowhere and disappearing before he could make sense of them.

What stayed with him most was not only that his friend died, but his conviction that he had become the kind of person he did not recognize. He had come to believe that in those minutes he had acted against his own values, and he returned home certain that something essential in him had been damaged. He said, in the flat, definite way he said many things, that he had no future worth picturing. Among college friends now building careers and dating and making plans, Mateo felt permanently set apart, as if everyone else had remained inside ordinary life while he had crossed into somewhere he could not come back from. That belief colored the way he held the memory itself: instead of settling into a story with a beginning and end, it remained a collection of brutally clear images that seemed to arrive charged with accusation, each piece seeming to confirm his sense that he was not the man he should have been.

In the months after discharge, those memories began intruding in ordinary places. At work, walking across the open trading floor toward a conference room, he would suddenly feel the same exposed vulnerability he had felt on that road overseas. A bright expanse of windows, the long distance between desks, even the empty atrium in the lobby could bring up a fragment—the dust, the shouting, the sight of his friend going down—so abruptly that he would stop mid-step and feel disoriented. Because the memories came in isolated, vivid pieces and never in an order he could control, he became increasingly determined not to give them any opening. He started taking narrower side corridors whenever he could, lingering by walls, choosing enclosed stairwells over the open lobby, and timing lunch to avoid the busiest common areas.

His view of himself pushed the avoidance further. Mateo was certain that if he spoke about what happened, other people would hear what he already believed about himself: that he had failed, that something shameful had been revealed in him, that he no longer belonged with people who had not done what he had done. He stopped his mother when she gently mentioned the soldier who had died. He ignored texts from a former squadmate who wanted to catch up. When coworkers asked routine questions about his military service, he gave clipped answers and changed the subject. Anything that reminded him of the man he lost—a memorial post online, a holiday honoring service members, even a song they used to play in the barracks—was quickly shut off or scrolled past. Avoiding those reminders felt like the only way to keep grief from breaking through and exposing how little future he believed he had.

Over time the pattern narrowed his life. At the office he was still technically competent, but colleagues noticed how often he declined team lunches held in the bright open plaza below the building, or how he positioned himself at the edge of meeting rooms nearest the door. Friends stopped inviting him out after he repeatedly refused. The less he talked and the more carefully he steered around reminders, the less chance he had to place the memory into any coherent order, and the more it returned as disconnected flashes. Each intrusion seemed to prove to him that he was stuck in the event and permanently outside everyone else’s world. By the time he sought help, he was exhausted by the effort of managing his days around what he could not see, hear, mention, or remember clearly. What finally brought him in was a morning at work when crossing the open floor triggered such a vivid fragment that he had to lock himself in a restroom stall until it passed. He said he was afraid that this was all his life would be from now on—avoiding, bracing, and keeping silent—but some part of him still hoped there might be a way to remember what happened without being condemned by it every time it returned.
